_comment: Patterns that must never appear in a tracked file of this public repository.
Copy to redaction.json and fill in. redaction.json is gitignored — the patterns
themselves name internal systems, so the list is company information too.
REQUIRED, not optional. guard-company-content.py blocks git add/commit/push with
exit 2 while redaction.json is missing, unreadable, or holds zero usable patterns,
and a single pattern that fails to compile blocks too (it names which one). It used
to skip the content check instead, which made 'looked at no patterns at all' arrive
in the same shape as 'matched no pattern' — and this file is gitignored, so that was
the state of every fresh checkout. The path check runs with or without this file.
Each entry is a Python regex, matched case-insensitively against staged diff text.
Set "ignoreCase": false on a pattern whose signal is capitalization (CamelCase
symbols); otherwise re.I turns [A-Z]\w+Service into a match for 'microservice'.
The last three entries are the shapes that actually leak when a skill, a hook or a
script documents its own reasoning with a measured example. Two of them carry no
company information and so are real rather than placeholders: a path ending in a
source extension, and a class name in the legacy naming convention.
legacy-source-path does not match a path under `.claude/`. This repository's own
tracked files - a PHP template we ship, a skill quoting its path - are not company
content, and a guard that blocks them is a guard someone switches off. The lookbehind
is what does it: a path segment preceded by `.`, `/` or a word character cannot start
a match, so a path under a dot-directory has no legal starting point, while a relative
or absolute path into the legacy tree still has one at its first segment.
legacy-tree-dir is the third and it does need filling in, because a service
directory has no extension to recognize it by - only its name. Build it from
workspace.json's legacy.treeMarker and legacy.services so the two cannot drift.
Anchor both ends on a non-word character: the trailing anchor is what keeps a
directory named `x` out of a match for `xy`, and the leading one must allow `/`
or an absolute path containing the directory goes unmatched.
